title: A neighbor's day of atonement
hook: Jews keep Yom Kippur as a day of fasting and repentance, in their own way and with their own meaning

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was aequinoctium, equal night, and a scale that's never perfectly even. Your line was equal light.

One autumn evening, synagogues fill for a day the Torah sets apart. Some people wear white. Those who keep the fast eat and drink nothing from that evening until the stars come out the next night, when a long blast of the ram's horn ends the day. This is Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement. Leviticus calls it a sabbath of solemn rest. It isn't ours to borrow. But a good neighbor can learn what it is, and let it ask a question of their own life.
screen: `AN AUTUMN EVENING, SYNAGOGUES FILL.` → `EVENING TO NIGHTFALL, NO FOOD OR WATER.` → `A NEIGHBOR'S HOLY DAY.`

segments.voice: First, the source. In the book of Leviticus, the tenth day of the seventh month is set apart. In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, the people are told: "ye shall afflict your souls." Jewish tradition has long understood that as fasting and holding back from certain comforts, and the day is spent largely in prayer, from the evening service called Kol Nidre to the closing service, Neilah. Second, the inner work. At its center is the Hebrew word teshuvah, often translated repentance, though it comes from the root for returning. Turning back. Jewish teachers, Maimonides among them, describe recognizing a wrong, regretting it, setting it right where possible, and resolving to do differently. Third, other people. The Mishnah, an early collection of Jewish law, says Yom Kippur brings atonement for wrongs between a person and God, but for wrongs between one person and another, not until you've made peace with the person you wronged. So it's a custom, in the days before, to call, write and apologize. The day doesn't skip the phone call. Fourth, what a neighbor can take, carefully. Not the fast, the prayers or the meaning, which belong to the people who keep it. Only the question it leaves in the air for anyone watching with respect: have I looked honestly at my year? Is there someone I owe a word to? The Stoics had their own version, Seneca's nightly review, coming again soon. That's a different thing, from a different place, and it doesn't stand in for this one.
screen: `LEVITICUS: YE SHALL AFFLICT YOUR SOULS.` · `TESHUVAH: TURNING BACK.` · `WRONGED A PERSON? MAKE PEACE FIRST.` · `A NEIGHBOR'S QUESTION, NOT A BORROWING.` · then, large: `HONEST REVIEW.`

segments.voice: In your own way, look back over the past year, not to punish yourself, just to see: where you did well, and one place you fell short of who you meant to be. If a person is connected to it, picture them, and ask whether a word from you, an apology or a thank-you, might be owed. You don't have to decide now; just let the honest picture stand.
Teshuvah, the Hebrew word at the heart of Yom Kippur, meaning turning back: recognizing a wrong, regretting it, and resolving to do differently. Today's word.
Your line: honest review. An honest look comes before any setting right. Day six hundred sixty-eight, done.

howItsDone: On Yom Kippur many Jews fast from one evening until nightfall the next and spend much of the day in synagogue prayer; in the days before it, many seek out people they have wronged to apologize.
